translations.text: These days are called Letaniae, that is, Prayer-days. On these days we must pray for an abundance of our earthly crops, and for health and peace for ourselves, and, what is still more, for the forgiveness of our sins.
We read in books that this observance was established at the time when a great earthquake happened in a city which is called Vienne,
and churches and houses fell, and wild bears and wolves came and devoured a great part of the people, and the king's palace was burned up with heavenly fire.
Then Bishop Mamertus ordered a fast of three days, and the affliction then ceased; and the custom of that fast continues everywhere in the faithful Church.
They took the example of that fast from the people of Nineveh. That people was very sinful: God meant to destroy them, but they pleased him with their repentance.
God spoke to a prophet who was called Jonah: "Go to the city of Nineveh, and preach there the words that I tell you."
Then the prophet became afraid, and wanted to flee from God's sight, but he could not. He went then to the sea, and boarded a ship.
When the sailors had come out to sea, God sent them a great wind and storm, so that they despaired of their lives.
Then they threw their goods overboard, and the prophet lay and slept. Then they cast lots among themselves, and prayed that God would reveal from where that misfortune had come upon them.
Then the prophet's lot came up. They asked him who he was, or where he meant to travel.
He said that he was the servant of God, who created sea and land, and that he had meant to flee from God's sight.
They said, "What shall we do about you?" He answered, "Throw me overboard; then this affliction will cease."
They did so, and the storm was stilled, and they offered their sacrifice to God, and went on their way.
God then prepared a whale, and it swallowed the prophet, and carried him to the land to which he was supposed to go, and spewed him out there.
Then the word of God came again to the prophet, and said, "Arise now, and go to the great city of Nineveh, and preach as I told you before."
He went, and preached that God's wrath was descending upon them if they would not turn to God.
Then the king rose from his royal throne, and cast off his precious robe, and put haircloth on his body, and ashes upon his head, and ordered that every man should do the same;
and both the people and the suckling children, and the beasts as well, tasted nothing for three days.
Then, because of that conversion, in that they turned away from evil, and because of that strict fast, God had mercy on them,
and he would not destroy them, as he had earlier burned with heavenly fire the citizens of the two cities, Sodom and Gomorrah, for their sins.
We must also on these days perform our prayers, and follow our relics out and in, and praise Almighty God with zeal.
We will now explain to you this gospel which has just now been read here: "Quis vestrum habebit amicum" [Which of you shall have a friend], and so on.
"The Saviour said to his disciples, Which of you is there who has a friend, and goes to him at midnight, and says," and so on.
Saint Augustine expounded this gospel and said that the night signified the ignorance of this world. This world is filled with ignorance.
Now therefore everyone must rise from ignorance and go to his friend, that is, he must turn to Christ with all zeal, and ask for the three loaves, that is, faith in the Holy Trinity.
The Almighty Father is God, and his Son is Almighty God, and the Holy Spirit is Almighty God; not three Gods, but they all are one Almighty God, indivisible.
When you come to these three loaves, that is, to the understanding of the Holy Trinity, then you have in that faith life and food for your soul,
and you may also feed another guest with them; that is, you may teach the faith to another friend who asks you for it.

He said "guest" because we are all guests in this life, and our homeland is not here at all; rather, we are here like travellers. One comes, another goes; one is born, another passes away and makes room for him.
Now, therefore, everyone should desire the faith of the Holy Trinity, because that faith will bring him to eternal life.
We will speak more about faith later, because the exposition of this gospel has a good connection to it.
The master of the household, who had gone to his rest with his children, is Christ, who sits in heaven with his apostles, and with the martyrs, and with all the saints whom he gathered in this life.
We must call to Christ and ask for the three loaves. Even if he does not grant them to us at once, we must not give up our prayer because of that.
He delays, and yet he will give. He delays so that we will be eager for it, and will hold God's gift as precious.
Whatever a person gets easily is not nearly as precious as what is gained with difficulty.

The Saviour said, "If he keeps on knocking, then the master of the household gets up because of the other man's calling and grants him what he asks for, not out of friendship, but because of his persistence."
He said "Not for friendship's sake" because no one would be worthy either of the faith or of eternal life if God's mercy toward mankind were not greater.
Now we must knock and cry out to Christ, because he will grant our request, just as he himself said: "Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you."
To each one who asks earnestly and does not give up his prayer, God grants eternal life.
Then he told another parable: "What father will give his child a stone if it asks him for bread? Or a snake if it asks for a fish?
or a scorpion, if he asks for an egg?" God is our Father through his mercy, and the fish signifies faith, the egg holy hope, and the bread true love.
God gives these three things to his chosen ones, because no one can have God's kingdom unless he has these three things.
If he wants to come to God's kingdom, he must believe rightly, and have hope in God, and true love toward God and toward people.
The fish signifies faith, because it is the fish's nature that the more the waves toss it, the stronger it becomes and the more it thrives.
So too with the faithful person: the more he is afflicted for his faith, the stronger that faith becomes, provided he is sound.
If he gives way under persecution, then it is not faith but pretence.
The egg signifies hope, because birds do not breed as other animals do; first there is an egg, and afterwards the mother, in hope, broods the egg into a chick.
Likewise our hope has not yet arrived at what it hopes for, but is like an egg. When it has what was promised to it, it will be a bird.
The loaf signifies true love, which is the greatest of all virtues, just as bread is the foremost of all foods.
Faith is a great power, and true hope is great; yet love surpasses them, because it lasts forever into eternity, and the other two come to an end.
We now believe in God and we hope in him. Later, when we come to his kingdom, as he promised us, faith will be ended, because then we will see what we now believe.
Our hope will also be ended, because we will have what we hoped for before. But love never fails; that is why it is now the best of them.
In the gospel the snake is set against the fish. In the form of a snake the devil deceived Adam, and he now constantly fights against our faith; but our protection depends on our Father.
The scorpion, which is set against the egg, is venomous and strikes people dead with its tail.
The things that we see in this life are perishable; those that we do not see, and that are promised to us, are eternal:
stretch your hope toward it, and wait until you have it. Do not look back; fear the scorpion that poisons with its tail.
The person who looks back is the one who despairs of God's mercy; then his hope is poisoned by the scorpion's tail.
But both in hardships and in good fortune and in misfortune we must say, as the prophet said, "I will praise my Lord at all times."
Whether things go well for us in the body or badly, we must always thank God for it and bless his name; then our hope will be protected against the creature's sting.
The stone is set against the bread, because hard-heartedness is opposed to true love. Hard-hearted is the person who will not help others out of love where he is able to.
The gospel said, "If you, who are evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give a good spirit to those who ask him."
What are the good things that people give their children? Temporary good things, such as the gospel mentioned: bread, and fish, and an egg.
These things are good in their measure, because the earthly body needs that food.
Now, just as you, wise people, will not give your children a serpent instead of a fish, so our heavenly Father will not give us the devil's faithlessness if we ask him to give us true faith.
And just as you will not give your child a scorpion instead of an egg, so God will not give us despair instead of hope.
And just as you will not give your child a stone instead of bread, God also will not give us hardness of heart instead of true love.
But the good heavenly Father gives us faith, and hope, and true love, and causes us to have a good spirit, that is, a good will.
We must consider the words he said, "You who are evil." We are evil, but we have a good Father. We have heard our name: "You who are evil."
But who is our Father? Almighty God. And of what sort of people is he the Father? It is plainly said: of evil people. And what sort of Father is he?
He of whom it is said, "No one is good but God alone." He who is always good makes us, who are evil, into good people, if we turn from evil and do good.
The man Adam was created good, but through his own choice and the devil's urging he became evil, and so did all his offspring. Whoever is sinful is evil, and no one alive is without some sin.
But our good Father cleanses and heals us, as the prophet said: "Lord, heal me, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved."
Whoever wants to be good should call upon him who is always good, so that he may make him good.
A man has gold, which is good in its measure; he has land and wealth, which are good.
But the man is not good because of these things unless he does good with them, as the prophet said, "He distributed his goods and gave them to the poor, and his righteousness endures for ever."
He lessened his wealth and increased his righteousness. He lessened what he must leave behind, and what he will have for eternity is increased.
You praise the merchant who gets gold in exchange for lead, but you will not praise the one who gets righteousness and the kingdom of heaven in exchange for perishable money.
The rich man and the poor man are travellers in this world. Now the rich man carries a heavy burden of his possessions, and the poor man goes empty-handed.
The rich man carries more than he needs for his provisions on the journey; the other carries an empty bag.
Therefore the rich man must share his burden with the poor man. Then he lessens the burden of his sins and helps the poor man.
We are all God's poor. Let us therefore acknowledge the poor who ask of us, so that God may acknowledge us when we ask him for what we need.
Who are those who ask of us? Poor men, frail and mortal. From whom do they ask?
From poor men, frail and mortal. Apart from their possessions, those who ask there and those they ask from are alike.
How can you for shame ask God for anything, if you refuse your fellow man what you could very easily grant him?
But the rich man looks at his silken clothes and says, 'That beggar in his rags is not my equal.'
But the apostle Paul rebukes him to his face with these words: "We brought nothing into this world, and we cannot take anything away from here with us."
If a rich woman and a poor woman give birth together, and then they go away, you do not know whether a child is the rich woman's or the poor woman's.
Again, if someone opens the graves of dead people, you do not know whether the bones are the rich man's or the poor man's.
But greed is the root of all evils; and those who follow greed stray from the faith of God, and they fall into various temptations and harmful desires, which sink them into destruction.
It is one thing if someone is rich because his parents bequeathed possessions to him; it is another if someone becomes rich through greed.
This man's greed is accused before God, but not the other man's possessions, provided his heart is not set on fire with greed.
The apostle Paul gave a command about such men: "Command the rich not to be proud, and not to put their hope in their uncertain wealth;
but let them be rich in good works, and give to God's poor with a generous mind, and God will repay them a hundredfold for whatever one does for the poor out of love for him."
The rich man and the poor man are necessary to each other. The wealthy man is made for the sake of the poor man, and the poor man for the sake of the wealthy.
It is fitting for the wealthy man that he spend and share out; it is fitting for the poor man that he pray for the giver. The poor man is the way that leads us to God's kingdom.
The poor man gives more to the rich man than he takes from him. The rich man gives him bread that is turned to dung, and the poor man gives the rich man eternal life:
not he, however, but Christ, who said thus: "What you do for a poor man in my name, you do for me myself," who lives and reigns with the Father and with the Holy Spirit for ever without end. Amen.
